Good morning. This is the outer channel summary for the fourteenth of March. At four twelve this morning a bulk carrier of thirty-two thousand tonnes went aground in the outer approach channel while proceeding under pilotage at eight knots. All twenty-two crew are accounted for and no injuries have been reported. No pollution has been observed in the channel or at the anchorage. The hull was breached in two forward compartments, and both compartments were isolated within the hour. The vessel will be refloated on the following tide with the assistance of two harbour tugs and escorted to the roadstead for inspection. Until further notice the outer channel is closed to deep-draft traffic. Vessels awaiting a berth should remain at the anchorage and keep a listening watch on channel sixteen.

People always want a single cause, and there almost never is one. The tidal window was revised at twenty-two hundred the night before. The bridge team was told by radio, and I have no doubt that they heard it, because two of them repeated the new time back. What never happened is the next step. Nobody entered the revision in the log, and nobody amended the passage plan. So when the ship left her berth six hours later, the plan on the chart table still described a tide that no longer existed. The under-keel clearance looked adequate on paper and was not adequate in the water. That is the whole finding. It is not about one careless officer. It is about a procedure that allowed a change to be spoken and never written.
